==English== ===Alternative forms=== * {{q|dialectal}} [[ter]] * {{q|contraction}} [[t']] * {{q|abbreviation}} [[2]] ===Etymology 1=== {{ety|en|id=particle|:inh|enm:to>|tree=1}} From {{inherited|en|enm|to}}, from {{inherited|en|ang|tō}}, from {{inherited|en|gem-pro|*tō}} ~ {{m|gem-pro|*ta}}, from {{inherited|en|ine-pro|*de}} ~ {{m|ine-pro|*do||to}}. Cognate with {{cog|sco|tae}}, {{m|sco|to||to}}, {{cog|frr|to}}, {{m|frr|tö}}, {{m|frr|tu||to}}, {{cog|stq|tou||to}}, {{cog|nds|to||to}}, {{cog|nl|toe}}, {{m|nl|te||to}}, {{cog|de|zu||to}}, {{cog|fy|ta||to}}. Non-Germanic cognates include {{cog|sq|ndaj||towards}}, Irish {{m|ga|do||to, for}}, Breton {{m|br|da||to, for}}, Welsh {{m|cy|i||to, for}}, {{cog|ru|до||to}}. {{doublet|en|too}}. ====Pronunciation==== =====Stressed===== * {{enPR|to͞o}}, {{IPA|en|/tuː/}} ** {{a|en|UK}} *** {{IPA|en|[tu̟ː]|[tʰʊw]|a=RP}} *** {{IPA|en|/tiː/|a=Northumbrian}} *** {{IPA|en|[tʰʉw]|a=SSB}} ** {{IPA|en|[tʰu̟(ː)]|a=US}} ** {{IPA|en|[t(ʰ)u̟ː]|a=CA}} ** {{IPA|en|[tʰʉː]|a=AU,NZ}} * {{audio|en|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Vealhurl-to.wav|a=Southern England}} * {{audio|en|En-us-two.ogg|a=GA}} * {{homophones|en|too|two}} * {{rhymes|en|uː|s=1}} =====Unstressed===== {{rfap|en|(US, after a vowel) (before a vowel) }} * {{IPA|en|q=before a consonant|/tə/|/tʊ/}} ** {{IPA|en|[ɾə]|a=US|q=after a vowel}} ** {{IPA|en|/tɪ/|a=Northumbrian}} ** {{audio|en|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Vealhurl-to2.wav|a=Southern England}} ** {{audio|en|En-au-play to win.ogg|"play to win"|a=Australian}} * {{IPA|en|q=before a vowel|/tʊ/|/tu(ː)/}} ** {{a|en|UK}} *** {{IPA|en|[tʊ(w)]|a=RP}} *** {{IPA|en|/tɪv/|a=Northumbrian}} *** {{IPA|en|[t(ʰ)ʉw]|a=SSB}} ** {{IPA|en|[tʊ(w)]|[tu̟]|a=US}} ** {{IPA|en|[ɾʊ(w)]|[ɾu̟]|a=US,after a vowel}} ** {{IPA|en|[tʊ(w)]|[tu̟(ː)]|a=CA}} * {{IPA|en|/ʈʊ/|a=Indic,always}} ====Particle==== {{en-head|pcl}} # {{non-gloss|A particle used for marking the following verb as an [[infinitive]].}} #: {{ux|en|I want '''to''' leave.}} #: {{ux|en|He asked me what '''to''' do.}} #: {{ux|en|I have places '''to''' go and people '''to''' see.}} #: {{ux|en|'''To''' err is human.}} #: {{ux|en|Who am I '''to''' criticise? I've done worse things myself.}} #: {{ux|en|Precisely '''to''' get away from you was why I did what I did.}} #: {{ux|en|I need some more books '''to''' read and friends '''to''' go partying with.}} #: {{ux|en|Those '''to''' avoid death [[ended up]] being exiled.}} #: {{ux|en|He fled to India, never '''to''' return.}} #: {{ux|en|I woke up '''to''' find my name plastered on every [[front page]].}} #: {{ux|en|If he lets you down, he'll have me '''to''' [[reckon with]].}} #* {{RQ:Pope Essay on Criticism|text='''To''' err, is human; '''to''' forgive, divine.}} #* {{RQ:Shakespeare Hamlet|3|1|text='''To''' be, or not '''to''' be: that is the question: / {{...}}}} #* {{quote-journal |en |date=April 10, 2011 |author=Alistair Magowan |title=Aston Villa 1 - 0 Newcastle |work=BBC Sport |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/eng_prem/9446263.stm |page= |passage=To that end, the home supporters were in good voice '''to''' begin with, but it was Newcastle who started the game in the ascendancy, with Barton putting a diving header over the top from Jose Enrique's cross.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20260903052909/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/eng_prem/9446263.stm|archivedate=3 September 2026}} # {{non-gloss|As above, with the verb implied.}} #: {{ux|en|"Did you visit the museum?" "I wanted '''to''', but it was closed."}} #: {{ux|en|If he hasn't read it yet, he ought '''to'''.}} # {{non-gloss|Used to indicate an obligation on the part of, or a directive given to, the subject.}} #: {{ux|en|You are '''to''' go to the store and buy a bottle of milk.}} =====Derived terms===== {{col4|en|{{l|en|finna}} ({{l|en|fixing to}}) |{{l|en|gonna}} ({{l|en|going to}}) |{{l|en|gotta}} ({{l|en|got to}}) |{{l|en|hafta}} ({{l|en|have to}}) |{{l|en|oughta}} ({{l|en|ought to}}) |{{l|en|supposta}} ({{l|en|supposed to}}) |{{l|en|usta}} ({{l|en|used to}}) |{{l|en|wanna}} ({{l|en|want to}}) }} =====Translations===== {{rfc|en|Sense 1 is not the English infinitive morpheme, that would be ''[[-∅]]''. The sentence "I could eat." contains a verb in the infinitive but no ''to''. Rather, ''to'' is a particle that is used in conjunction with an already (zero-)marked infinitive. The box below, however, seems to contain a random mix of translations of the infinitive marker ''[[-∅]]'' (e.g. {{m+|de|-en}}, {{m+|ro|-a}}, {{m+|tr|-mek}}) and the particle ''to'' (e.g. {{m+|de|zu}}, {{m+|ro|a}}).}} {{trans-top|infinitive-marker}}{{multitrans|data= * Albanian: * Arabic: * Armenian: * Assamese: * Azerbaijani: * Bengali: * Bulgarian: * Catalan: * Cornish: * Czech: * Danish: * Dutch: * Esperanto: * Estonian: * Faroese: * Finnish: * French: * Galician: * German: * Greek: * Hawaiian: * Hebrew: * Hindi: * Hungarian: * Icelandic: * Ido: * Igbo: * Indonesian: * Irish: * Italian: * Ladin: * Ladino: * Latin: * Latvian: * Limburgish: * Lithuanian: * Macedonian: * Malay: * Maltese: * Neapolitan: * Nepali: * Norwegian: * Persian: * Polish: * Portuguese: * Punjabi: * Romanian: * Russian: {{qualifier|suffix}} {{tt|ru|-ать}}, {{tt|ru|-ять}}, {{tt|ru|-еть}}, {{tt|ru|-ить}}, {{tt+|ru|-ти}}, {{tt|ru|-уть}}, {{tt|ru|-чь}}, {{tt+|ru|-ть}} * Scots: * Serbo-Croatian: * Sicilian: * Slovak: * Slovene: * Spanish: * Swahili: * Swedish: * Talysh: * Tamil: * Turkish: * Ukrainian: * Veps: * Volapük: * Võro: * Votic: * Zulu: {{trans-bottom}} {{trans-top|particle used with infinitives}} * Spanish: {{trans-bottom}} {{checktrans-top}} * German: {{tt|de|es tun}} {{qualifier|may left out}} * Italian: {{tt+|it|da}} {{qualifier|+ infinitive verb}}, {{tt+|it|per}} {{qualifier|+ infinitive verb}} }} {{trans-bottom}} ====Conjunction==== {{en-head|con}} # So as to bring about or elicit (an effect or outcome). #: {{ux|en|He made several bad-taste jokes '''to''' groans from the audience.}} #: {{ux|en|I tried complaining, but it was '''to''' no effect.}} #: {{ux|en|'''To''' everyone's great relief, the tuneless carol singers finally ceased their warbling.}} # ==English== {{wp}} ===Pronunciation=== * {{IPA|en|/ˈðeɪ̯/|a=RP,GA}} ** {{audio|en|En-uk-they.ogg|a=RP}} ** {{audio|en|En-us-they.ogg|a=GA}} * {{IPA|en|[ˈðæ̝ɪ̯]|a=AU}} * {{IPA|en|/ðə/|a=Northumbrian,unstressed}} * {{rhymes|en|eɪ|s=1}} * {{hyph|en|they}} * {{hmp|en|day|the|aa1=th-stopping|aa2=Northumbria}} ===Etymology 1=== {{etymon|en|id=pronoun|:inh|enm:þei|tree=1}} {{word|en|ine|só}} From {{inh|en|enm|þei}}, borrowed in the 1200s from {{der|en|non|þeir}},{{R:American Heritage Dictionary}} plural of the demonstrative {{m|non|sá}} which acted as a plural pronoun. Displaced native {{ncog|enm|he}} from {{ncog|ang|hīe}} — which vowel changes had left indistinct from {{m|enm|he|t=he}} — by the 1400s,{{R:Etymonline}}Otto Jespersen, ''Growth and Structure of the English Language'' being readily incorporated alongside native words beginning with the same sound ({{m|en|the}}, {{m|en|that}}, {{m|en|this}}). Used as a singular pronoun since 1300, e.g. in the 1325 ''Cursor Mundi''. The Norse term (whence also {{cog|is|þeir|t=they}}, {{cog|fo|teir|t=they}}, {{cog|da|de|t=they}}, {{cog|sv|de|t=they}}, {{cog|nn|dei|t=they}}) is from {{der|en|gem-pro|*þai|t=those}} (from {{der|en|ine-pro|*só|*to-|that}}), whence also {{cog|ang|þā|t=those}} (whence obsolete English {{dbt|en|tho|notext=1}}), {{cog|sco|thae}}, {{m|sco|thai}}, {{m|sco|thay|t=they; those}}, {{cog|swg|dia|t=they}}. The origin of the determiner {{m|en|they|t=the, those}} is unclear. The ''OED'', ''English Dialect Dictionary'' and ''Middle English Dictionary''{{R:MED Online|entry=thei|pos=pron|id=MED45106|accessdate=2016-01-28}} define it and its Middle English predecessor {{m|enm|thei}} as a demonstrative determiner or adjective meaning “those” or “the”. This could be a continuation of the use of the English pronoun {{m|en|they}}'s Old Norse etymon {{m|non|þeir}} as a demonstrative meaning “those”, but the ''OED'' and ''EDD'' say it is limited to southern, especially southwestern, England, specifically outside the region of Norse contact. ====Pronoun==== {{en-pron|desc=third-person, nominative case, usually plural, sometimes singular|objective case|them|possessive|their|possessive noun|theirs|reflexive|themselves|or reflexive singular|themself}} # {{senseid|en|third-person plural nominative}} {{lb|en|the third-person plural nominative}} A group of entities previously mentioned. {{defdate|since 13th c.}} #: {{ux|en|Fred and Jane? That's just what '''they''' want you to think.}} # {{lb|en|bridge}} The opponents of the side which is [[keep score|keeping score]]. #: {{ant|en|we}} =====Usage notes===== * {{sense|singular pronoun}} Usage of ''they'' as a singular pronoun began in the 1300s and has been common ever since, despite attempts by some grammarians, beginning in 1795,Anne Bodine, ''Androcentrism in Prescriptive Grammar: Singular 'they', Sex-indefinite 'he', and 'he or she''', in ''Language in Society'', v. 4 (1975), pages 129–146 to condemn it as a violation of traditional ([[Latinate]]) agreement rules. Some other grammarians have countered that criticism since at least 1896.William Malone Baskervill and James Witt Sewell's ''An English Grammar'' (1896) says singular ''they'' is "frequently found ''when the antecedent includes or implies both genders''. The masculine does not really represent a feminine antecedent"; it furthermore recommends changing it to ''he'' or ''she'' "''unless both genders are implied''". (Italics in original.) ''Fowler's Modern English Usage'' (third edition) notes that it "is being left unaltered by copy editors" and is "not widely felt to lie in a prohibited zone". Some authors compare use of singular ''they'' to widespread use of singular ''you'' instead of ''thou''.Michael Reed, ''Tech Book 1'' {{ISBN|0956081312}}, ''Note about pronoun usage'', page 9: "Singular ''they'' can introduce some ambiguity because the antecedent of the pronoun “they” could theoretically be a male or female [... but] English has survived the loss of pronouns such as ''thou'' (singular ''you'') despite the consequent potential for ambiguity."John McWhorter, ''Word on the Street: Debunking the Myth of a Pure Standard'' (2009, {{ISBN|0786731478}}: "In this light, our modern grammarians' discomfort with singular ''they'' is nothing but this comical intermediate stage in an inevitable change, as misguided and futile as the old grumbles about singular ''you''." See {{w|singular they|Wikipedia's article on singular ''they''}} for more; see also the usage notes about {{m|en|themself}}. (Compare {{m|en|he}}.) * {{sense|singular pronoun}} In the past, ''they'' tended to be used of a generic or unidentified person, or someone who was not previously named or identified as male or female. It has increasingly been used to refer to an unnamed person even if the gender of the person is known. * {{sense|singular pronoun}} Even when used as a singular pronoun, in standard English singular ''they'' uses the same verb conjugations as plural ''they'', like singular and plural ''you'': "George, you ''were'' {{small|[not ''was'']}} here when the masked figure ran past, ''were'' {{small|[not ''was'']}} they wearing red or blue?" * {{sense|singular pronoun}} Infrequently, ''they'' is used of an individual person of known, binary gender. See [[Citations:they#Pronoun: single person of specified sex or gender|citations]]. * {{sense|singular pronoun}} Infrequently, ''they'' is used of an individual animal which would more commonly be referred to as ''[[it]]''. See [[Citations:they#Pronoun: single animal or plant|citations]]. * {{sense|indefinite pronoun}} ''[[one|One]]'' is also an indefinite pronoun, but the two words do not mean the same thing and are rarely interchangeable. "They" refers to people in general (hence the expressions {{m|en|they say}}, {{m|en|so they say}}, {{m|en|you know what they say}}), whereas "one" refers to one person (often such that what is true for that person is true for everyone). ''You'' may also be used to refer to people in general; such use of that pronoun is called the [[generic you#Noun|generic ''you'']]. *: ''They say beauty is in the eye of the beholder.'' *: ''One may say, "Beauty is in the eye of the beholder."'' *: ''You may say, "Beauty is in the eye of the beholder."'' =====Alternative forms===== * {{alt|en|They}} {{q|honorific}} * {{alt|en|dey}}
